own_scenes.place: Londres, Ibiza y el campo inglés
own_scenes.desc: En 1988 el acid house tomó Londres y los DJs de Detroit empezaron a tocar en clubes ingleses; Mark Moore (S’Express) reunió un círculo transatlántico con Peter «Baby» Ford. En Rhythm King, con Bomb the Bass de Tim Simenon, Colin Faver y Eddie Richards, hicieron un pop de baile subversivo que llegó al número uno; Sarah Gregory pintó un mural en el Music Institute y grabó con Carl Craig en un piso de Londres un disco que nunca salió (el sello se pasó al pop-rock en 1992). Las fiestas salieron de Shoom, Spectrum y The Trip a granjas y almacenes y se llamaron raves. El éxtasis, traído de Ibiza (el «Balearic»), se fusionó con la música; la prensa habló de LSD, Top of the Pops vetó la palabra «acid» y Radio One prohibió «Chikki Chikki Ahh Ahh». En Detroit, castigado por el crack, nadie bebía ni se drogaba (el Music Institute solo servía zumo y agua); May y Marshall Jefferson se levantaron del New Music Seminar de 1989 tras oír al productor de los Happy Mondays reconocer que eran camellos. Los DJs tuvieron que pinchar los momentos extáticos («Strings of Life», «Can You Feel It») y la prensa no supo ver la innovación de May o Craig. El Reino Unido acabó prohibiendo las fiestas masivas, que volvieron a los clubes.

refs.q: “Techno was some kind of revolutionary musical form—that I still believe. It was crossing cultures, crossing the Atlantic and everything.”
refs.para: Within a year, Detroit DJs were getting booked in English clubs regularly, and weekend junkets turned into extended vacations and career explorations as they began to make friends with similar artists. One of these was the well-established Mark Moore, the producer behind the sample-pop-acid house sensation S’Express. Moore was also the center of a growing transatlantic clique that included English techno artist Peter “Baby” Ford, among others. “[We] were a small group of people that took it [techno and acid house] in quite a deep way,” says Ford. “Techno was some kind of revolutionary musical form—that I still believe. It was crossing cultures, crossing the Atlantic and everything.”
refs.chapter: Cap. 4: Nation to Nation: Finding a Home in Britain’s Rave Culture, 1988–1991

refs.q: “I’ve never seen such a group of teetotalers—no one drank and no one took drugs,” notes Sarah Gregory.
refs.para: The negative connotations of “acid” became as troubling to Detroit’s techno artists as they were to the English establishment. Drugs were almost completely absent in Detroit’s techno scene, small as it was, and the artists were undoubtedly a bit shocked to find their music fused with any kind of drug-related experience. The Music Institute didn’t even serve alcohol, only juice and water. “I’ve never seen such a group of teetotalers—no one drank and no one took drugs,” notes Sarah Gregory. Some, like May, were immediately and vocally at odds with techno’s association with drug culture, and especially with those within the dance music community who helped perpetuate it. Following the surge in Detroit’s crack cocaine sales through the early and mid-1980s, and the lives lost as a result, drugs had become a much more serious matter to techno’s producers. For them, drugs carried deadly connotations.
refs.chapter: Cap. 4: Nation to Nation: Finding a Home in Britain’s Rave Culture, 1988–1991

refs.q: The crowd was rocking the music, not the other way around.
refs.para: What was clear was that music journalists were having a hard time covering the new music scene, struggling between judging techno and its ilk for their functionality and for their purely artistic merit. In this arena, much of Detroit’s musical innovation went undetected—especially that of Derrick May and Carl Craig. Critics argued that conceptual epics like Rhythim Is Rhythim’s “The Beginning” took too long to get to the point. The crowd was rocking the music, not the other way around.

podcast.title: Aesthetic in Early Video Games
podcast.body: Even before PlayStation, many Amiga computer titles in the late 1980s and early 1990s already featured a distinct rave aesthetic, indicating an early connection between electronic dance music and video game culture. "muchos titulos para ordenadores amiga ya respiraban la estética Rafe."

podcast.title: Cultural Foundation for Early Electronic Music
podcast.body: Rave culture provided the foundational environment for the rise of British electronic music genres like hardcore breakbeat, jungle, and early drum and bass. It fostered a vibrant scene of clubs, pirate radio, and illegal parties that championed these high-energy sounds. "fortemente ligado a la cultura rave."

podcast.title: Emergence from Acid House Culture
podcast.body: Rave culture developed in England between 1988 and 1989, directly stemming from the Acid House scene and influenced by Ibiza's clubs. These events featured continuous music played all night in clubs, with ecstasy becoming an integral part of the experience. The parties, often extending throughout the weekend, served as a haven for diverse young people who adopted rave culture as a life philosophy. "dando pie a la cultura Raif. Los clubs pasaron a pinchar esa música sin pausa durante toda la noche y el ex-Tasis se convirtió en un elemento inseparable de la escena."

srcs.episode: Chill Out: La pausa que necesitaba la electrónica

podcast.title: Explosion in Manchester
podcast.body: The Haçienda nightclub in Manchester served as a ringside seat to the "explosion" of rave music, as well as the rise of the DJ as a star, becoming a central hub for this cultural phenomenon in the late 1980s and early 1990s. "The balconies and stairwells were ringside seats to the explosion in rave music and mad chester in the rise of the DJ as star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Extreme 90s European Culture
podcast.body: European rave culture in the late 1980s and early 1990s was characterized by its extreme and aggressive nature, stemming from the radicalization of American House and Techno. This culture was so intense that it "swept away an entire generation" due to pervasive drug use, a situation that the Big Beat movement later sought to soften. "esa cultura electrónica rey de los 90 rasos con una generación entera, o sea si llevó una generación completa por culpa de las drogas."

srcs.episode: The Chemical Brothers. Padres de la cultura BIG BEAT

podcast.title: Influence on 2000s Alt Rock
podcast.body: "Old school raves" were identified as one of the many dance influences that artists in the 2000s incorporated into alt rock, showcasing the genre's eclectic and fragmenting musical directions. "These acts blended alt rock sensibilities with a million different types of dance influences, from old school raves to disco to house to R&B to certain elements of hip hop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Initial Rejection of Slower Tempos
podcast.body: Within the 90s rave culture, there was a strong preference for very heavy and hardcore electronic music, which initially led to the rejection of slower, more hip hop-influenced sounds like Big Beat. "dentro de la cultura rey blajente estaba muy por la electrónica muy heavy, muy hardcore."

srcs.episode: The Chemical Brothers. Padres de la cultura BIG BEAT

podcast.title: Keygen Music Influence
podcast.body: Keygen music, often electronic and fast-paced with accelerated tempos, shared similarities with Rave music. This energetic style helped to create a sense of excitement and cinematic hacker experience for users entering activation keys. "Esta música solía ser el electrónica y rápida, con tiempos acelerados musíilar a la música Rave o el Trance..."

srcs.episode: El oscuro origen de la música de los KEYGEN

podcast.title: Leading Scene in Later 1980s
podcast.body: The Rave scene is mentioned as one of the later emerging movements that took the lead in popularity and innovation within the electronic music landscape after the mid-1980s. "más tarde la escena Reis y el IBM."

srcs.episode: Por qué KRAFTWERK es la banda más influyente de la historia?

podcast.title: Prominence in the UK
podcast.body: Rave culture was highly popular and significant in the UK during the late 1980s, providing a receptive environment for bands whose sound incorporated elements of modern dance, like The Stone Roses. "It was the perfect combination for the times, especially since Rave and House were so big in the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Target of New York City Cabaret Law (1980s)
podcast.body: During the 1980s, New York City's cabaret law was invoked by Rudy Giuliani to target rave events. This led to dance parties being pushed into unsafe, unlicensed underground warehouses and basements, as the law prohibited dancing in establishments serving alcohol without a special license. "In the 1980s Rudy Giuliani used this law to crack down on hip-hop venues and raves, forcing dance parties into dangerous underground unlicensed warehouse and basements."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Mind-Blowing Facts About Music in 60 Minutes: 2017 Edition

podcast.title: UK Scene and Techno/House Popularity
podcast.body: The rave scene in the United Kingdom played a crucial role in popularizing both techno and house music. Derrick May's "Strings of Life" achieved "in-done" status within this scene, and British record agents actively sought to export these sounds to European discos. "La Terra, donde estaban haciendo la escena Rafe... en la nueva escena Rafe, se habían convertido en estrellas."
